Messages.Author: Raille
Messages.Body:
Player A has a Trophy Hunting Ground in play.

Player B use's reformation (dom. Burn 1 blood to steal a hunting ground.) to
steal it.

Is this legal play?

Where does, or how is the change assigned?

If the stolen THG is burned or otherwise removed to the ash heap, does it go
back to the original card owner?

Raille

Messages.Author: The Lasombra
Messages.Body:
On Tue, 2 May 2006 22:15:44 -0400, "Raille" <rai...@yahoo.com> wrote:

>Player A has a Trophy Hunting Ground in play.

>Player B use's reformation (dom. Burn 1 blood to steal a hunting ground.) to
>steal it.

>Is this legal play?

Perhaps.

http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/index.php?line=Preview_KMW_Trophy

"Once placed on a vampire, a trophy cannot be moved again."

Looks like the specific card text over-rides this rule.

>Where does, or how is the change assigned?

The controller of the acting minion will decide, same as any other
ambiguous change of control. See the parallel with Location Based
Equipment.

Equipments which are Locations (Loquipment):
# Loquipment may be put on any ready minion if moved in an ambiguous
fashion (by Disputed Territory, e.g.). If the new controller has no
minions, the locquipment is burned. (Note: currently all moves are
ambiguous - TOM). [RTR 19960112]

>If the stolen THG is burned or otherwise removed to the ash heap, does it go
>back to the original card owner?

Always.

1.1.2 of the online rulebook.

Burn: When a card is "burned," it is placed into its owner's discard
pile (the discard pile is called the "ash heap" for this reason).

http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/rulebook/

Trophy: Hunting Ground [KMW:R]
Cardtype: Master
Master. Trophy. Hunting Ground.
During your untap phase, the vampire with this card gains 2 blood from
the blood bank. A vampire can gain blood from only one Hunting Ground
card each turn.
Artist: Avery Butterworth

Cardtype: Action
Discipline: Dominate
+1 stealth action. Requires a ready anarch.
[dom] (D) Burn 1 blood to steal a hunting ground.
Artist: Attila Adorjany

Messages.Author: Fred Scott
Messages.Body:
"Joshua Duffin" <jtdu...@yahoo.com> wrote in message

news:4bv1fbF...@individual.net...

>> "Once placed on a vampire, a trophy cannot be moved again."
>
> Well, card text can override most of the rules in the rulebook.

I've always thought that was a fundamentally unworkable concept:

Card A (action): This action can absolutely never be blocked no
matter what.

Card B (reaction): This reacting minion blocks the acting minion
no matter, despite any text on the action card.

I mean, I'm sure the conundrum can be worked out and rulings can
be issued and all that, but when you just say "card text overrides
rulebook rules", you create the potential for conflicts like
this since it doesn't give any clue _which_ card's text is more
important than another's.

Ultimately, card text doesn't actually override rules in a CCG
like they say. Ultimately, card text that contradicts rules
just means the actual CCG rules are extended in a usually
unwritten fashion to accommodate the new card functions. When
conundrums like this are created, LSJ (or the equivalent
authority in whichever game you're talking about) gets going
and issues rulings which extend the unwritten rules to a
written format - though still often not actually causing the
rulebook itself to be altered - and which resolve whatever
paradox has occurred.

Fred

Actually it is. My point is that "card vs. rules" doesn't describe
all the issues that come up. In fact, "card vs. card" is quite
possible and the statement, "Card text can override rules in the
rulebook" doesn't cover the situation. It's not unworkable because
it's wrong in and of itself. It's unworkable because it's
incomplete.

> But the rules don't say that, so we're safe there.

As far as I know, the rules don't say anything.

> There is a ruling regarding card text vs. card text, though, which is
> that the most recent effect wins out. Like Clan Impersonation vs. Clan
> Impersonation. (Note that some cards prohibit later cards from being
> used -- like cards that set range.)

With all due respect, I don't believe that addresses the conunumdrum I
posed above. I believe the situation would require some kind of a
ruling.

>> Ultimately, card text doesn't actually override rules in a CCG
>> like they say. Ultimately, card text that contradicts rules
>> just means the actual CCG rules are extended in a usually
>> unwritten fashion to accommodate the new card functions. When
>
> Tomayto, tomahto.

I disagree. Effectively, the claim from Josh's quoted statement is
that cards go outside "rules space" (for want of a better term) and
alter it. My dispute is that there is _no_ such thing as going
outside rules space. Just that new cards which allow some new effect
actually (de facto) alter and widen the rules space. The distinction
is in the misunderstanding that cards which contradict rules all exist
in some kind of a vacuum. They don't. I believe that that's why
mistakes often get made in the design of cards by designers, when
they forget about what other cards do as they design new cards and
create problematic and/or unintended interactions between cards. And
by players who don't always realize that a new effect is more
complex and involved than they first thought when they read a
relatively simple passage on a card. I think my way of stating the
situation (above) is a better way to conceptualize the relationship
between cards and rules.

> Wake actually overrides the rules about tapped vampires not being able
> to block. Strained Vitae Supply actually overrides the rules about how
> much stealth a hunt action has.

And Spying Mission overrides the payment a prey would make to satisfy
a bleed, as does Archon Investigation. If a predator wants to play the
former and a prey wants to play the latter on the same bleed, how is
conflict resolved? Well, of course, a method has been well-established.
But I'll bet it was never considered until after AI was printed. Even
if it was, there have been thousands of other such interactions that
weren't - that is my point.

> There may indeed be a few instances of conundrums. But that does not
> mean the concept is fundamentally unworkable.

I don't think "few" describes it very well. I'm sure you do as good
a job as anyone could about thinking the implications of new effects
through before you approve them for printing. But, certainly correct
me if I'm wrong, I don't believe you can say you've only been
surprised by unexpected interactions just a "few" times over the
years.

I suppose you can dust off my distinction as "tomayto, tomahto" in
that it doesn't fix the problem, obviously. But I still think it's
a stronger way of describing reality. Which makes it a useful
thing in my book.

Fred
